A branch current sensor measures total current upstream of the connector contactors. A controller communicates with the connector interfaces and contactors over an isolated local bus.

The branch current sensor is an independent safety input. If measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command for a verification interval, the controller opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit. A contactor is not reclosed until its connector current sensor reports zero, the control-pilot interface reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired. A welded-contactor condition is recorded when connector current remains above a leakage threshold after an open command. The controller then inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates a local fault indicator.

The controller can receive remote schedules and authorizations through a network interface, but it stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. It does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. This prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

content.content:
1	Sites that install several electric-vehicle charging connectors frequently supply those connectors from a single electrical branch. The branch is protected at an allowable aggregate current, referred to herein as a branch limit, that is commonly lower than the sum of the individual connector ratings. Installing a branch large enough for every connector to draw its full rating at the same time is often impractical, because the cost of the additional service capacity, conductors, and protective devices can exceed the cost of the charging equipment itself.
2	
3	Charging equipment therefore has to share a fixed amount of current among connectors that could collectively demand more. The signalling mechanism ordinarily available for that purpose is the control pilot presented to each vehicle, which advertises a maximum current that the vehicle is permitted to draw. Control-pilot signalling is advisory in nature. The value advertised on the pilot is a command, not a measurement, and the current actually drawn depends on the behaviour of the vehicle receiving it. A vehicle may respond slowly, may respond only in coarse steps, may hold a previous value while its own thermal or state-of-charge logic settles, or may not reduce at all. Control that assumes the commanded value is the delivered value therefore has no way to detect the case in which the branch remains loaded above its limit after a reduction has been ordered, and that case is precisely the one in which the branch protective device is at risk of operating and removing service from every connector on the branch.
4	
5	A further difficulty arises because the branch usually carries loads other than charging. Lighting, building services, and other equipment on the same branch consume part of the allowable aggregate current, and that consumption varies through the day. Allocation that divides the full branch limit among the connectors, without accounting for the varying non-charging portion of the branch load, either overcommits the branch or forces the installer to configure a permanently conservative limit that wastes capacity for most of the day.
6	
7	Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.
8	
9	Charging equipment is additionally exposed to conditions that are specific to its power path and its installation. A contactor whose contacts have welded continues to pass current after an open command has been issued, so an allocation scheme that treats an open command as removal of the load will continue to believe that capacity has been released when it has not. Site communication to a remote management system is not continuous, so equipment that depends on a remote authority for both authorization and current limits either stops serving vehicles when the link fails or continues without a governing limit. Multi-connector equipment is also wired by hand, and a transposition between the logical identifier of a connector and the physical contactor and sensor channel that serve it causes a current limit intended for one connector to be applied to another, which defeats the allocation entirely while leaving every individual component apparently functional.
10	
11	There remains a need for charging control that treats the current actually present on the branch and at each connector as the governing quantity, that keeps the branch within its limit even when a vehicle does not honour a reduced pilot command, that allocates the genuinely available portion of the branch limit in a way that corrects accumulated inequality between sessions, and that remains safe and operable when the site link is down, when a contactor has welded, and when the installation wiring map has not been independently confirmed.
12

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.
2	
3	Overview of the system
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.
6	
7	The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.
8	
9	A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.
10	
11	The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.
12	
13	A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.
14	
15	The connector station
16	
17	FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126.
18	
19	The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and the first control-pilot interface 124 reports whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.
20	
21	Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another.
22	
23	The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.
24	
25	The edge controller
26	
27	FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a nonvolatile memory 132 and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 carries out the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.
28	
29	The edge controller 100 is further coupled to a local fault indicator 134 and to a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.
30	
31	For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is a stored current value that is assigned to the session at that connector before any further distribution of the available charging current is made. 74

76

78

Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and the first control-pilot interface 124 reports whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a nonvolatile memory 132 and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 carries out the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 is further coupled to a local fault indicator 134 and to a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is a stored current value that is assigned to the session at that connector before any further distribution of the available charging current is made. The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted.

Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the signed local authorization token does not authorize, and a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

input.summary:
LEDGER RESULT: The draft tracks the disclosure closely. Every claim limitation, every numbered part, and essentially every specific structure, relationship, operating condition and variant in the description and figure briefs traces to an exact affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md (the conversation's single USER passage is verbatim identical to the disclosure, so it adds no further authority). Two items are reported below: one geometric self-contradiction inside the FIG. 4 brief, and one definitional gloss in the description that has no affirmative source passage.

TRACED (representative): Claim 1's connector stations (contactor + connector current sensor + control-pilot interface) -> "Each connector has a controllable contactor, a connector current sensor, a control-pilot interface, and a local connector identifier"; branch sensor upstream of the contactors -> "A branch current sensor measures total current upstream of the connector contactors"; isolated local bus -> "communicates with the connector interfaces and contactors over an isolated local bus"; branch limit below the sum of ratings -> "whose allowable aggregate current is lower than the sum of the connector ratings"; the four stored per-connector values -> "stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value"; the allocation arithmetic (subtract measured non-charging branch load and configurable safety reserve; minimum sustaining first; remainder by energy deficit; send limit on pilot; verify with connector sensor) -> disclosure para. 2 verbatim; the staged sequence (reduced pilot command, verification interval, one-at-a-time opening in a stored shedding order until below the branch limit) -> disclosure para. 3. Claims 2/10 (three reclose permissives incl. randomized recovery delay), 3/11 (leakage threshold, welded condition, inhibit other contactors on the same branch, local fault indicator), 5-7/12-13 (network interface, signed local authorization token and last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory, continue authorized sessions during outage, refuse newly connected sessions, tamper-evident local sequence uploaded when communication returns), and 8/14 (service input, one low-energy pilot transition at a time, store association only after the sensed channel agrees) each map to an exact disclosure sentence. The separability paragraph (08 line 89) traces to "Offline authorization, welded-contactor isolation, tamper-evident records, and installation mapping are supported additional features."

NUMERALS: All 23 numerals in draft/numerals.md are used in the description and appear on exactly one figure list each in a consistent sense; no numeral designates two parts, and no figure brief uses a numeral absent from the table. Numeral gaps (116, 118, 128, 130) are unused, not orphaned.

FIGURES: The four briefs match the four Brief-Description entries and depict only disclosed structure. Rectangles, straddling sensor boxes and the two isolation strokes are labelled "shown schematically" in the briefs and remain shape-neutral in the claims and description. The one convention statement that could carry substance - FIG. 2's note that the order of contactor 120 and sensor 122 along the power path "is a drawing convention" - is correctly confined to the figure brief and is not echoed in the application text; the description (08 line 17) asserts no order. No "by way of example", "any closed outline", or shape-justifying embodiment language appears anywhere in the application text.

SECTION LINES: No sectional or source-view figures are specified, so the repeated-designation check is not applicable; there is nothing to reconcile.

TERMINOLOGY / INTERNAL CONSISTENCY: Claims and description use identical terms throughout ("assigned limit", "verification interval", "stored shedding order", "leakage threshold", "randomized recovery delay", "configurable safety reserve", "available charging current", "minimum sustaining current", "energy-deficit value", "signed local authorization token", "last accepted branch limit", "tamper-evident local sequence", "low-energy pilot transition"). Claim 5's restatement of "the independent branch-current safety process" as the reduced pilot command plus ordered opening matches 08 lines 47-53. The FIG. 4 flow (206 -> 208 -> 210, 210 -> 200 on success, 210 -> 212, 210 -> 214, 212 -> 200) matches the described process, apart from the geometry problem reported below. Dependency chain (4 on 3; 6 and 7 on 5; 13 on 12) is well formed. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction to the drafter, unresolved alternative, or internal comment remains in draft/ or figures/.

FORMALITIES: Title matches the brief's working title. Cross-reference and government-support sections read "Not applicable.", consistent with the brief's "No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development." No means-plus-function language. Abstract is a single paragraph of about 143 words with no reference numerals.

CITATIONS: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no documents, and the Background accordingly contains no [REF:...] citations - it is generic problem framing only, which needs no inventor support. As the brief notes, no prior-art search was run, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete; a later review should confirm the Background's characterizations against whatever art is eventually supplied.

findings.title: FIG. 4 brief specifies a "horizontal" connector between two steps that its own stacking places at different heights
findings.detail: The brief stacks four rectangles in the left column (200, 202, 204, 206, top to bottom) and three in the right column (208, 210, 212, top to bottom), then instructs that step 206 be joined to step 208 by a horizontal line. Step 206 is the fourth rectangle of a four-box column and step 208 is the first rectangle of a three-box column, so the two cannot lie at the same vertical position while the remaining right-column boxes (210, 212) and the lower-right rectangle 214 also fit within the drawing area. As written the three instructions cannot all be satisfied, and a renderer must silently override one of them. This is a geometry inconsistency inside the brief only; the flow it expresses (allocation verification followed by the pilot reduction step) is consistent with the detailed description at draft/08-detailed-description.md lines 43 and 49.
findings.evidence: figures/FIG-4.md: "Four rectangles are stacked in a column in the left half of the drawing area. From the top of the column downward these are the available-charging-current determination step 200, ... and the limit transmission and connector current verification step 206." / "Three rectangles are stacked in a column in the right half of the drawing area. From the top of that column downward these are the pilot reduction step 208, the ordered contactor shedding step 210, and the reclose permissive step 212." / "A horizontal line runs from the right side of the limit transmission and connector current verification step 206 to the left side of the pilot reduction step 208 with an arrowhead pointing at it."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-4.md, replace the third geometry bullet with: "A line leaves the right side of the limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, runs to the right clear of every rectangle, turns upward, and ends at the left side of the pilot reduction step 208 with an arrowhead pointing at that rectangle." No change to the application text is needed.

findings.title: Description defines "requested current" as unconstrained demand; the disclosure names the stored value but never defines it
findings.detail: The disclosure lists "a requested current" among the four per-connector stored values but nowhere says what it represents. The description supplies a specific characterization - the current the session would take if capacity were unconstrained - which is a definition of a claimed term (claims 1 and 9 both recite "a requested current") that has no affirmative passage behind it. No other source passage narrows the gap: the only other reference to the requested value is the disclosure's rejection of request-proportional sharing, which appears nowhere in the inventor text at all. The fix is to state the term in source-faithful language rather than to supply an unsourced definition.
findings.evidence: Candidate wording (draft/08-detailed-description.md line 31): "The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained." Nearest source passage (input/disclosure.md line 7, identical at input/conversation.md line 9): "The controller stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value." - the value is named but not defined, and no affirmative passage anywhere in the disclosure or conversation describes it as unconstrained demand.
findings.fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md line 31, replace "The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained." with "The requested current is a stored current value for the session at that connector." No claim change is required, since claims 1 and 9 recite only "a requested current".

A branch current sensor measures total current upstream of the connector contactors. A controller communicates with the connector interfaces and contactors over an isolated local bus.

At each allocation interval, the controller subtracts measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. It first assigns the minimum sustaining current to sessions that can receive it, then distributes remaining current according to energy deficit. The controller sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface and verifies the resulting connector current with the corresponding current sensor.

The branch current sensor is an independent safety input. If measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command for a verification interval, the controller opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit. A contactor is not reclosed until its connector current sensor reports zero, the control-pilot interface reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired. A welded-contactor condition is recorded when connector current remains above a leakage threshold after an open command. The controller then inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates a local fault indicator.

The controller can receive remote schedules and authorizations through a network interface, but it stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. During a network outage it continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process. It does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.

A service input permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the corresponding connector current sensor. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. This prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

The disclosed essential relationship is closed-loop allocation using both per-connector current sensing and independent upstream branch sensing, with staged reduction followed by ordered contactor shedding when branch current does not respond. Offline authorization, welded-contactor isolation, tamper-evident records, and installation mapping are supported additional features.

content.content:
1	Sites that install several electric-vehicle charging connectors frequently supply those connectors from a single electrical branch. The branch is protected at an allowable aggregate current, referred to herein as a branch limit, that is commonly lower than the sum of the individual connector ratings. Installing a branch large enough for every connector to draw its full rating at the same time is often impractical, because the cost of the additional service capacity, conductors, and protective devices can exceed the cost of the charging equipment itself.
2	
3	Charging equipment therefore has to share a fixed amount of current among connectors that could collectively demand more. The signalling mechanism ordinarily available for that purpose is the control pilot presented to each vehicle, which advertises a maximum current that the vehicle is permitted to draw. Control-pilot signalling is advisory in nature. The value advertised on the pilot is a command, not a measurement, and the current actually drawn depends on the behaviour of the vehicle receiving it. A vehicle may respond slowly, may respond only in coarse steps, may hold a previous value while its own thermal or state-of-charge logic settles, or may not reduce at all. Control that assumes the commanded value is the delivered value therefore has no way to detect the case in which the branch remains loaded above its limit after a reduction has been ordered, and that case is precisely the one in which the branch protective device is at risk of operating and removing service from every connector on the branch.
4	
5	A further difficulty arises because the branch usually carries loads other than charging. Lighting, building services, and other equipment on the same branch consume part of the allowable aggregate current, and that consumption varies through the day. Allocation that divides the full branch limit among the connectors, without accounting for the varying non-charging portion of the branch load, either overcommits the branch or forces the installer to configure a permanently conservative limit that wastes capacity for most of the day.
6	
7	Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.
8	
9	Charging equipment is additionally exposed to conditions that are specific to its power path and its installation. A contactor whose contacts have welded continues to pass current after an open command has been issued, so an allocation scheme that treats an open command as removal of the load will continue to believe that capacity has been released when it has not. Site communication to a remote management system is not continuous, so equipment that depends on a remote authority for both authorization and current limits either stops serving vehicles when the link fails or continues without a governing limit. Multi-connector equipment is also wired by hand, and a transposition between the logical identifier of a connector and the physical contactor and sensor channel that serve it causes a current limit intended for one connector to be applied to another, which defeats the allocation entirely while leaving every individual component apparently functional.
10	
11	There remains a need for charging control that treats the current actually present on the branch and at each connector as the governing quantity, that keeps the branch within its limit even when a vehicle does not honour a reduced pilot command, that allocates the genuinely available portion of the branch limit in a way that corrects accumulated inequality between sessions, and that remains safe and operable when the site link is down, when a contactor has welded, and when the installation wiring map has not been independently confirmed.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.
2	
3	Overview of the system
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.
6	
7	The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.
8	
9	A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.
10	
11	The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.
12	
13	A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.
14	
15	The connector station
16	
17	FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126.
18	
19	The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and the first control-pilot interface 124 reports whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.
20	
21	Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another.
22	
23	The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.
24	
25	The edge controller
26	
27	FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a nonvolatile memory 132 and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 carries out the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.
28	
29	The edge controller 100 is further coupled to a local fault indicator 134 and to a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.
30	
31	For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is a stored current value that is assigned to the session at that connector before any further distribution of the available charging current is made. The energy-deficit value is a stored value that represents the energy by which the session at that connector has been under-served.
32	
33	Allocation at each allocation interval
34	
35	FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.
36	
37	At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.
38	
39	At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each such session is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.
40	
41	At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.
42	
43	At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.
44	
45	The branch current sensor as an independent safety input
46	
47	The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.
48	
49	At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the staged sequence, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.
50	
51	At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.
52	
53	The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.
54	
55	The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.
56	
57	Recovery after shedding
58	
59	At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.
60	
61	Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.
62	
63	On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.
64	
65	Welded-contactor isolation
66	
67	At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.
68	
69	When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors prevents further controllable load from being placed on the branch while the welded contactor continues to conduct. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.
70	
71	Operation during a network outage
72	
73	The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted.
74	
75	During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the signed local authorization token does not authorize, and a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started.
76	
77	Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.
78	
79	Installation mapping through the service input
80	
81	A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.
82	
83	The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. In response to the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.
84	
85	The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found during installation instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.
86	
87	General considerations
88	
89	The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the installation mapping described above, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.
90	
91	The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, and the shedding order are values stored by the edge controller 100.
92	
93	The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.
94

Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each such session is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the staged sequence, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors prevents further controllable load from being placed on the branch while the welded contactor continues to conduct. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the signed local authorization token does not authorize, and a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. In response to the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found during installation instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the installation mapping described above, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, and the shedding order are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

findings.title: Summary says the branch current sensor is not a term in the allocation arithmetic, while the description uses its measurement in that arithmetic
findings.where: draft/06-summary.md paragraph beginning "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than..."; conflicts with draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraphs describing the branch current sensor ("Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream..."), the determination step 200 ("The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current..."), and the safety-input paragraph ("It is not merely a further term...")
findings.detail: The Summary makes an absolute exclusion: the branch current sensor is an independent safety input "rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic." The description, however, states that the branch current sensor 104 "reports the measured branch current" to the edge controller 100, that the current it measures "includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114," and that "The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114" - which is the quantity subtracted at the available-charging-current determination step 200. The branch measurement therefore does enter the allocation arithmetic. The description itself uses the correct hedged form ("It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200"), so the Summary is the outlier. The inventor source says only "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input" and does not exclude it from the allocation arithmetic.
findings.evidence: Summary: "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic." Description: "The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114." Description: "It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path..." Disclosure: "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input."
findings.fix: In draft/06-summary.md replace "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic." with "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input: beyond supplying the branch measurement used in the allocation arithmetic, it governs a protection process that acts on the power path."

findings.title: Stated reason why the branch measurement includes the non-charging load does not follow from the recited sensor location
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, Overview of the system, paragraph beginning "A branch current sensor 104 measures total current..."
findings.detail: The text reasons that the branch measurement includes the non-charging load current because the sensor is upstream of the connector contactors. Being upstream of the connector contactors says nothing about the non-charging load 114; inclusion follows only if the branch current sensor 104 is also upstream of the non-charging load 114. FIG. 1 does depict exactly that (all three drop lines, including the one to the non-charging load 114, descend from the branch conductor 102 at points to the right of the branch current sensor 104), and the disclosure supports it by reciting that the sensor "measures total current," so the topology is source-supported; only the stated causal link is defective.
findings.evidence: Description: "Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114." FIG-1.md: "Three vertical drop lines descend from the branch conductor 102 at points to the right of the branch current sensor 104... The rightmost rectangle is the non-charging load 114." Disclosure: "A branch current sensor measures total current upstream of the connector contactors."
findings.fix: Replace that sentence with: "The branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors and upstream of the non-charging load 114, so the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114."

findings.title: Definition of the requested current as the unconstrained draw is not in the inventor source
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, The edge controller, paragraph beginning "For each active connector of the plurality..."
findings.detail: The description defines the stored requested current as "the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained." The disclosure lists "a requested current" among the values stored for each active connector and never characterizes it as the draw the session would take absent a capacity constraint. No affirmative USER passage supplies that meaning; the nearest source passage is the bare enumeration of stored values. The gloss adds an operating characterization of a stored value that no claim requires, so it can be removed without affecting scope.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained." Nearest source (disclosure and conversation, identical text): "The controller stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value." No further mention of the requested current appears anywhere in the disclosure or conversation.
findings.fix: Replace that sentence with: "The requested current is a stored value that represents the current requested for the session at that connector."

findings.title: Sizing condition asserted for the verification interval is not in the inventor source
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, paragraph beginning "At an ordered contactor shedding step 210..."
findings.detail: The description asserts a condition on the length of the verification interval: it "is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it." The disclosure recites the verification interval only as the period after which persistence of an over-limit branch measurement triggers shedding, and never states any requirement on its duration. No affirmative USER passage supports the sizing condition. Claim 1 and claim 9 recite only that the verification interval "has elapsed," so removing the assertion leaves the claims unaffected.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it." Nearest source (disclosure and conversation, identical text): "If measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command for a verification interval, the controller opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit."
findings.fix: Replace that sentence with: "The verification interval is the period that is allowed to elapse after the reduced pilot command before the measured branch current is re-evaluated."

findings.title: Summary says the branch current sensor is not a term in the allocation arithmetic, while the description uses its measurement in that arithmetic
findings.where: draft/06-summary.md paragraph beginning "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than..."; conflicts with draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraphs describing the branch current sensor ("Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream..."), the determination step 200 ("The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current..."), and the safety-input paragraph ("It is not merely a further term...")
findings.detail: The Summary makes an absolute exclusion: the branch current sensor is an independent safety input "rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic." The description, however, states that the branch current sensor 104 "reports the measured branch current" to the edge controller 100, that the current it measures "includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114," and that "The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114" - which is the quantity subtracted at the available-charging-current determination step 200. The branch measurement therefore does enter the allocation arithmetic. The description itself uses the correct hedged form ("It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200"), so the Summary is the outlier. The inventor source says only "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input" and does not exclude it from the allocation arithmetic.
findings.evidence: Summary: "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic." Description: "The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114." Description: "It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path..." Disclosure: "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input."
findings.fix: In draft/06-summary.md replace "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic." with "The branch current sensor is an independent safety input: beyond supplying the branch measurement used in the allocation arithmetic, it governs a protection process that acts on the power path."

findings.title: Sizing condition asserted for the verification interval is not in the inventor source

findings.detail: The description asserts a condition on the length of the verification interval: it "is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it."
